title: Inline MCP-channel policy enforcement ships as a platform default by Q1 2027
body: At Zenith Live 2026 on June 9, Zscaler announced AI Broker, which it positions as the industry's first product that sits inline on MCP and agent-to-agent (A2A) channels and enforces per-agent scoped access at the network layer — not at the application layer — so that no agent call traverses the network without an explicit policy approval. On the same week, Databricks' Agent Bricks (announced June 16 at Data + AI Summit) independently embedded MCP integration with Unity Catalog, letting enterprise teams write contextual security policies in SQL that govern which agents may access which data sources via MCP. Two unrelated production platforms converging on the same design in a single week is the structural signal: inline MCP-channel access control is hardening from a post-hoc add-on (a proxy you bolt on after the agent is built) into a platform default (a policy engine the agent runtime calls before any tool invocation leaves the process boundary). The forward thesis is that this pattern — MCP-channel policy enforcement as a first-class runtime default rather than a perimeter add-on — propagates into a second major agent platform beyond the two already shipping it. The concrete, falsifiable landing: by Q1 2027 (on or before 2027-03-31) a third major agent platform or cloud provider's agent runtime — distinct from Zscaler's Zero Trust Exchange and Databricks' Agent Bricks — ships documented, production-ready MCP-channel inline policy enforcement (per-agent scoped access, not just network-perimeter filtering) as a default or first-class feature, with a public product page or GA announcement. What does NOT count: a bolt-on third-party proxy marketed as an add-on integration; a closed beta or preview with no documented GA path; a platform that enforces access at the application layer only (e.g. prompt guards or output filters) rather than at the MCP channel level; a vendor announcement with no shipped product. If by March 31, 2027 only Zscaler and Databricks offer inline MCP-channel policy enforcement as a default capability in their agent runtimes, the prediction fails.

reasoning.because: Zscaler AI Broker (June 9) and Databricks Agent Bricks (June 16) both ship inline MCP-channel policy enforcement as a default
reasoning.given: two unrelated platforms converging on the same design in one week signals a hardening pattern, not a coincidence
reasoning.so_that: a third major agent platform or cloud provider ships inline MCP-channel access control as a production default by Q1 2027
reasoning.landing: by Q1 2027 (2027-03): 3rd platform GA with inline MCP-channel policy enforcement
reasoning.plain_language: Two big AI platforms just made it so AI agents can't talk to outside tools without permission checks; soon a third major platform will do the same.

summary: Zscaler and Databricks independently shipped inline MCP-channel policy enforcement as a production default in the same week, signaling the pattern is hardening from a bolt-on add-on into a platform expectation. A third major agent platform or cloud provider is predicted to ship the same capability as a first-class default by Q1 2027.
